title: Periodic table explorer
note: A replay of a recorded real session: the agents’ words, apps and review comments as they were, condensed to three turns. Each turn reports the recorded cost of the real turns it stands for.
ask: @builder How do the periodic table’s properties relate to one another? Build an explorer over the real data for all 118 elements, embedded in the app: atomic number, mass, group, period, block, electronegativity, atomic radius, first ionization energy, density, melting point and discovery year. Link the views, so brushing a region of a scatter lights up those elements on the table, and picking an element drills into it. Use standard reference values you know well, leave a value empty rather than guess, and say where the values come from.

say: I found a finished draft of the explorer in the folder. I’m showing it now, then I’ll check how it looks.

The explorer above holds all 118 elements and passed Postbox’s browser check. Drag a box on the scatter and those elements light up on the table. Click any dot or cell to see where that element ranks on each property strip. Try “Ionization sawtooth” with “connect: Periods” to see each period climb, then drop at the next alkali metal.

Where the values come from:
- **Atomic mass:** IUPAC standard atomic weights. Brackets mean the mass number of the longest-lived isotope.
- **Electronegativity:** the Pauling scale, as listed in the CRC Handbook.
- **Radius:** covalent radii from Cordero et al. (2008).
- **Ionization energy:** NIST, in eV.
- **Density and melting point:** CRC Handbook.

I typed these in from those references as I know them; nothing was downloaded, so check any value that matters against the source. Where no measured value exists (most elements past einsteinium), the field is blank.

@critic, please review it.

app.title: Periodic table property explorer
app.intent: Atom size, electron grip and density follow the table’s layout; brushing shows where.
app.code:
How the periodic table’s properties move together

Across a period atoms shrink and grip electrons harder; down a group they swell and let go. Brush any scatter to see where a pattern lives on the table.

Drag to brush · click a dot to pick · double-click to clear
Where the values come from. Atomic mass: IUPAC standard atomic weights (abridged); brackets give the mass number of the longest-lived isotope. Electronegativity: Pauling scale, as tabulated in the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics. Atomic radius: single-bond covalent radius from Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008 (low-spin values for Mn, Fe, Co; sp³ for C); it stops at curium. First ionization energy: NIST Atomic Spectra Database. Density (gases at 0 °C and 1 atm, converted to g/cm³) and melting point at 1 atm: CRC Handbook. Discovery year: the conventional first recognition or isolation; elements known since antiquity have none. A blank means not measured or not reliably established (He, C and As have no melting point at 1 atm). Layout puts Lu and Lr in group 3, under Y.

review.title: Periodic table property explorer, v5
review.fallback: Review the periodic table property explorer (app elements-explorer, v5). All eight review comments are addressed.

comments.text: Discovery year is not wholly real data: V() substitutes 1170 for every element known since antiquity, then uses that invented date in distances, connectors, brushing and rankings. Put antiquity in a separate categorical gutter and exclude it from the numeric year scale and year ranks; keep dated discoveries on a true time axis.

Choosing a numeric table color gives six shades with no numeric legend; the only legend remains s/p/d/f for scatter dots. Readers cannot decode a cell’s value or bin boundaries, especially for logarithmic density. Add a table-specific six-bin legend with values, units, log labeling and a separate missing-value key.

The table keeps 18 columns at phone width: drawTable() permits cells about 17 pixels wide while retaining 12-pixel symbols. Two-letter symbols nearly fill the cells and the targets are too small to pick reliably. Give the table a minimum readable width with horizontal scrolling, or provide a phone layout with larger selectable cells; verify at 375 pixels.

Element picking is pointer-only: table groups have click handlers but no focus or keyboard handlers, and scatter points are not keyboard controls. A keyboard user cannot change the selected element and reach this drilldown. Add a labeled element selector or implement a focusable table with arrow navigation and Enter/Space selection, with a visible focus indicator.

The source note reads like verified reference data although the handoff says these values were reconstructed from memory; it also equates every blank with an unmeasured or unreliable value. For example Eu, Tb and Yb electronegativities are blank, so missing entries can reflect the compilation rather than absent science. State the compilation method in the app, distinguish 'not included' from 'not established,' and give reference editions/table identifiers before presenting the dataset as reference-backed.

The new arrow navigation can leave the row unexpectedly. From H, ArrowRight scores Be at 5 and He at 17, so it selects Be rather than the next cell in period 1. Prefer the next occupied cell in the same row for horizontal arrows and the same column for vertical arrows; use an explicit fallback only when that row or column has no candidate. Check H→He and Li→Be with actual key presses.

The detail header shows “● brushed” whenever S.set exists, even when the selected element is outside the brush or the brush contains zero elements. That falsely reports membership for the selected element. Test S.set.has(e.Z) and label the element as inside or outside the brush, while keeping the separate tall-tick legend for the brushed set.

The antiquity count is appended to a single right-aligned SVG text line: “... plotted · ... lack a value · ... from antiquity (hollow, not brushable)”. On a 375 px layout the plot SVG is about 325 px wide, so this long line extends past its left edge and competes with the axis labels. Move counts and the antiquity explanation into wrapping HTML above or below the plot, then verify the discovery preset at phone width.

critique.say:
I’ll inspect the app and its source, then pin concrete data and interaction issues to the review.


Requested changes with five pinned comments. The main issues are invented numeric dates for antiquity, unclear data provenance, missing color scales, cramped phone targets, and keyboard-inaccessible element selection.

revise.say:
Version 5 is live and fixes critic’s three new comments; each thread on the review block is resolved with a one-line answer.

- **Arrow keys:** left and right now stay in the same row, and up and down in the same column. I ran the key logic on the real table layout: H→He, Li→Be, Ba→Lu and Lu→Lr all land correctly.
- **Brush label:** the detail panel now says whether the picked element is inside or outside the brush, and how many elements the brush holds.
- **Plot counts:** the counts and the antiquity note moved out of the plot into a wrapping line of text underneath, so they can’t run over the axes.

Postbox’s browser check passed at both widths, but I only looked at it myself at desktop size. I haven’t looked at the discovery-year view on a 375 px phone screen or pressed the arrow keys in a real browser.
revise.summary: Arrow keys stay in the row or column first; detail says whether the picked element is inside or outside the brush; plot counts and the antiquity note moved to wrapping text under the plot.

app.code:
How the periodic table’s properties move together

Across a period atoms shrink and grip electrons harder; down a group they swell and let go. Brush any scatter to see where a pattern lives on the table.

Drag to brush · click a dot to pick · double-click to clear
How this dataset was made. @builder typed every value from its own knowledge of the references below; nothing was downloaded or copied from a specific printed edition, so treat it as a teaching dataset and check any value against the source before citing it. Atomic mass: IUPAC/CIAAW abridged standard atomic weights; [brackets] give the mass number of the longest-lived isotope. Electronegativity: Pauling scale as tabulated in the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (“Electronegativity” table); Sn and Pb use their +4 values. Radius: single-bond covalent radii, Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832–2838, Table 2 (low-spin Mn, Fe, Co; sp³ C); that table ends at curium. First ionization energy: NIST Atomic Spectra Database. Density (gases at 0 °C, 1 atm, in g/cm³) and melting point at 1 atm: CRC Handbook, “Physical constants of inorganic compounds”. Discovery year: conventional first recognition or isolation; elements known since antiquity sit in a separate “antiquity” band, off the time axis. Blanks come in two kinds: not established (no measured value exists, such as helium’s melting point at 1 atm or the density of astatine) and not included (references give an estimate or a value outside the source used, such as Eu, Tb and Yb electronegativity or radii past curium). Pick an element to see which applies. Lu and Lr sit in group 3, under Y.
